list.listitem: Typhoid and typhus fevers are infectious diseases that are rare within the United States, and are primarily seen in returning travelers. A
Relapses and chronic carrier states are seen in both typhus and typhoid fever. C
Prevention of typhus and typhoid fever in those traveling to endemic areas include safe food preparation, avoidance of vectors, and immunizations, especially for typhoid fever. C

background.definition: Typhoid fever is an acute systemic illness unique to humans caused by Salmonella typhi. Epidemic typhus fever is an acute infectious disease caused by Rickettsiae transmitted by a body louse from human to human. Endemic typhus fever (aka murine typhus) is an acute infectious disease caused by Rickettsiae in rodents which is passed to humans by rat fleas. Scrub typhus is an acute infectious disease caused by Rickettsiae transmitted to humans by chiggers.

list.listitem: There are approximately 350 typhoid cases per year in the United States.
There are less than 100 endemic typhus cases per year in the United States
Epidemic and scrub typhus are rare in the US, even in travelers.
There are 0.1 typhoid cases per one million travelers to Northern Europe.
Approximately 100 typhoid cases per one million travelers to high risk areas, especially Southern Asia.
Most cases in the United States occur in persons returning to their country of origin for a visit.

In typhoid fever, the patient might become a chronic carrier (up to 5%) which is defined as persistent stool excretion of the bacteria for longer than 1 year. The salmonella is carried in the gall bladder in those cases.
Epidemic typhus occurs primarily in refugee camps, war, famine-struck areas, and/or disaster areas.
Recrudescent disease can account for human outbreaks of typhus after years of the initial infection.
Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella typhi.
Epidemic typhus is caused by Rickettsiae prowazekii. The vector is the human body louse Pediculus humanus corporis.
Endemic typhus is caused by Rickettsiae typhi. The vector is the rat flea Xenopsylla creopis or cat flea Ctenocephalides felis.
Scrub typhus is caused by Orienta tsutsugamushi. The vector is Leptotrombidium deliense.
Typhoid fever: the incubation period is 5 to 21 days. Transmission of typhoid fever occurs by direct contact of the bacteria from another human or animal.
Typhus fever: the incubation period is 5 to 7 days. The only reservoir for typhus is humans.

Epidemic typhus: the incubation period is 7 to 14 days with duration of 10 to 18 days. the bacteria is carried in the bloodstream of the body louse and leaked into the surrounding tissue (causing the red louse color) and into the feces. The feces enter the human skin through the louse's bite or aerosolized into the air.

Endemic typhus: the incubation period is 8 to 16 days with duration of 8 to 16 days.the bacteria is carried in the bloodstream of the flea and leaked into the surrounding tissue and into the feces. The feces enter the human skin through the flea bite or aerosolized into the air.
Scrub typhus: the incubation period is 6 to 21 days with duration of 6 to 21 days. Chiggers inoculate organisms into the skin while feeding on the host.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Exposure to undercooked food and untreated water (typhoid)

list.listitem: Vaccination with either oral or intramuscular typhoid vaccines are recommended for travelers to high risk areas (e.g., south Asia, central and South America, Africa, Asia if consuming food and drink in areas of poor sanitation and hygiene). C

The injectable typhoid vaccine (aka Typhim Vi) is for ages greater than two years. The dose is 0.5 mL IM, which is given two weeks before departure. With this particular vaccine, you need a booster every two years. A

A randomized trial of the Vi polysaccharide typhoid conjugate vaccine (Vi-TCV) in 28,130 children 9 months to 12 years of age in Malawi was 81% effective and safe. A second study of this vaccine in 10,005 participants aged 9 months to 16 years in Nepal also found 82% effectiveness and good safety.

The oral typhoid vaccine (aka Ty21a or Vivotif Bema) is for ages greater than six years. The dose is one capsule every other day for four doses starting one week before departure. With this particular vaccine, you need a booster every five years. A

A multidose dose schedule of Ty21a prevents 33% to 50% of typhoid cases within 2 years of vaccination; no benefit was detected in year 3. A single injection of Typhim Vi has a 3-year cumulative efficacy of 55%. A currently unlicensed vaccine, Vi-rEPA, has a 50% to 96% efficacy for the two years after vaccination. A
Both provide vaccine-elicited immunity 14 days after receipt of the last vaccine dose with an overall efficacy of 50% to 80%. A

A Cochrane review concluded that the Typhoid Ty21a and Vi vaccines are efficacious in adults and children older than two years in endemic countries and that the Vi-rEPA vaccine is also efficacious, although data is only available for children.

In Malawi, a trial including children aged 9 months to 12 years, randomized to receive either a Vi-TT typhoid vaccine or a MenA vaccine, showed that the Vi-TT vaccine was 78.3% effective over 4.6 years in preventing typhoid with no vaccine-attributable deaths, though serious adverse events were noted in both groups.

Preventative measures against typhus including forming a barrier to typhus causing organisms. This includes applying insect repellants with DEET, wearing permethrin-coated clothing and sleeping under bed nets, and delousing clothing and bedding when necessary. C
Serologic tests for Salmonella agglutinins (aka febrile agglutinins) are not recommended. B
Serologic testing for typhus may be positive, but two samples are needed. The first sample is taken during the acute phase; the second sample is taken during the convalescent phase. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Not caused by Yersinia or Campylobacter
Rash not on palms or soles
Rash begins on trunk with eschar
Rash begins on trunk with eschar

list.listitem: Typhoid fever: 30% to 50% of patients with typhoid fever will develop a rose spot, which is a transient erythematous maculopapular rash on the anterior thorax or upper abdomen. The most common signs are nonspecific and can include fever (up to 21 days after exposure), generalized abdominal discomfort, bloating, early onset diarrhea followed by constipation, headache, malaise, confusion/lethargy, and anorexia. Some patients will have a dry cough. Other signs of typhoid include splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, cervical adenopathy, relative bradycardia, and conjunctivitis.

Typhus fever: there is acute onset of fever, chills, headache, myalgia/arthralgias, malaise, bradycardia, eschar at bite site, lymphadenopathy, and diffuse organ involvement (including the intestines, liver, heart, kidney, and brain).

Epidemic typhus: the maculopapular rash in epidemic typhus begins on the trunk at day 5; which initially changes to petechiae or becomes hemorrhagic followed by a brownish pigmentation. Other manifestations of epidemic typhus include photophobia, ocular pain, conjunctiva injection, and CNS manifestations in up to 80% of patients.

Endemic typhus: the maculopapular rash in endemic typhus begins on the trunk at days 3 to 5; and is discrete, sparse lesions without hemorrhage. Other manifestations of endemic typhus include nonproductive cough in 30% to 70% of patients with bibasilar rales, pulmonary infiltrates, pulmonary edema, or secondary infections.
Scrub typhus: there will be an eschar at the bite site followed by a maculopapular rash beginning on the trunk about day 5.

There are several proposed rapid tests for early diagnosis of typhoid fever, the newest (Typhidot-M) is an enzyme immunoassay that detects an IgM antibody against 50 KDa OMP antigen of Salmonella typhi. In two comparative studies, the test was more sensitive than the Widal test (91.4%-92.6% and 42.8%-34.1%, respectively). Typhidot was less specific than the Widal test in one study (37.5% and 42.8%, respectively) but more specific in the second study (90% vs. 85%, respectively).
The white count in typhoid fever is generally normal, however liver function tests can be elevated.
In typhus fever, there is serologic testing for rickettsia.
With typhus fever, there is an early leukopenia followed by leukocytosis.
When evaluating for typhus, you must obtain two samples: the first sample from when the patient is first evaluated (acute phase); the second sample at a later date (convalescent phase).

Other abnormal lab values for typhus fever include thrombocytopenia (up to 40%), increased hepatic transaminases (up to 60%), hyperbilirubinemia (20%), elevated BUN (31%), hyponatremia (severe cases), and hypoalbuminemia (severe cases).

For typhoid, attempt isolation of S. typhi from sputum, urine, or stool. If the cultures are negative, attempt isolation of S. typhi from blood. Bone marrow culture can be used if multiple blood cultures are negative or patient has had prior antibiotic therapy (90% sensitivity).
For typhus, the Weil-Felix serological reaction may be positive (low sensitivity and non-specificity).
For epidemic and endemic typhus, there is a four-fold rise or titer great than 1:320 on OX-19 or the following: any titer >1:128, IgM titer >1:400, IgG titers >1:960.
For scrub typhus, there is a four-fold rise in titer on OX-K.
For typhoid fever, first-line antibiotics include 3rd generation cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones (especially for multidrug resistant typhi).B
For typhus fever, the treatment of choice is doxycycline. B

In patients with severe scrub typhus, the combination of azithromycin and doxycycline for 7 days reduces the likelihood of death or persistent complications or fever more than either antibiotic alone.B

For acute cases of typhoid fever, cephalosporins have been the mainstay of treatment with the antibiotic of choice being ceftriaxone 1 to 2 grams IV for 14 days. For acute cases of typhoid fever, there has been debate about the use of fluoroquinolones over cephalosporins. One study with 3 trials showed reduced clinical failure with fluoroquinolones, but no difference in microbiologic failure or relapse.

In a Cochrane review, azithromycin was better than fluoroquinolones in reducing clinical failure and decreasing hospital length of stay in hospitalized patients with uncomplicated typhoid and paratyphoid fever (enteric fever).

For carrier states of typhoid fever, chloramphenicol 50 mg/kg divided four times daily for 6 weeks is recommended if the microbe is sensitive. If the microbe is resistant to chloramphenicol, either the combination of ampicillin (4-5 grams/day divided four times daily) and probenecid (2 grams/day divided four times daily) or ciprofloxacin (500 mg twice daily) can be used for six weeks.

For adults and children over 8 years with epidemic or endemic typhus fever, doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 to 5 days is the treatment of choice. Chloramphenicol 500 mg four times daily for 7 to 15 days can also be used. However, for scrub typhus, a randomized trial of 93 people in showed that azithromycin in a single dose was more effective than a week of doxycycline.

A study randomized 794 patients with severe scrub typhus to 7 days of doxycycline (200 mg twice on day 1 and then 100 mg/day), azithromycin (1000 mg on day 1 then 500 mg/day) or both. The combination of azithromycin and doxycycline for 7 days reduces the likelihood the composite of death or persistent complications or fever more than either antibiotic alone (33% vs 47% to 48%, p = 002, NNT = 8).
Cholecystectomy may be recommended for carriers of typhoid fever if antibiotics fail.
Offer the typhoid vaccine to all travelers to high risk areas.

The injectable typhoid vaccine (aka Typhim Vi) is for ages greater than two years. The dose is 0.5 mL IM, which is given two weeks before departure. With this particular vaccine, you need a booster every two years.

The oral typhoid vaccine (aka Ty21a or Vivotif Bema) is for ages greater than six years. The dose is one capsule every other day for four doses starting one week before departure. With this particular vaccine, you need a booster every five years.
Hospitalize the patient if severely ill or unstable vitals.

Complications of typhoid fever include intestinal hemorrhage and perforation of the distal ileum, chronic carrier state, seeding in the biliary tract, osteomyelitis (especially in sickle cell patients, SLE, and immunocompromised host), and endovascular infections.

Other rare complications of typhoid fever include endocarditis, pericarditis, meningitis, pancreatitis, hepatitic/splenic abscesses, orchitis, hepatitis, nephritis, myocarditis, pneumonia, arthritis, osteomyelitis, and parotiditis.

For typhoid fever, management of the hospitalized patient includes fluid and electrolyte support, strict isolation, serial KUBs to evaluate for bowel perforation, IV antibiotic treatment, and blood transfusions if needed for hemorrhage.

For typhus fever, complications for specific organs usually occur during the second week of infection. Management should be geared towards treatment of azotemia, meningoencephalitis, seizures, delirium, coma, myocardial failure, hyponatremia, hypoalbuminemia, hypovolemia, and shock.
Prognosis for typhus and typhoid are good with proper antimicrobial therapy and follow-up. B
Because typhoid vaccines have an efficacy of approximately 70%, enteric fever is still a possibility in patients who have been immunized. C
Recrudescent stage of epidemic typhus (aka Brill-Zinsser disease) can occur up to 40 years after initial infection. C
For typhoid fever, there is less than 2% mortality rate. However there is a 15% relapse rate with some antibiotics.
There is a 3% bowel perforation rate from typhoid fever.
For typhus fever, the mortality rate without treatment is 40% to 60% for epidemic typhus, 1% to 2% for endemic typhus, and up to 30% for scrub typhus.
The recrudescent stage of epidemic typhus (aka Brill-Zinsser disease) can occur up to 40 years after initial infection with low or absent titers of IgM Ab.
Prognosis is good with treatment for both typhus and typhoid.
Relapses for typhus fever may follow treatment especially if initiated within 48 hours.
Periodic follow-up should be done for both typhus and typhoid.
Offer the typhoid vaccine if traveling to endemic countries. The vaccines are 70% effective. Workers in high risk areas should also be vaccinated.

Advise should be given on proper food hygiene practices; treated water supplies; proper hand hygiene; adequate sanitation to dispose of human fecal waste; exclusion of infected people from handling food or providing health care; education on the risk of Salmonella infections from animal contact to prevent typhoid transmission.
Advise should also be given on using bug repellents, wearing long clothes, and avoiding bites by the vectors to prevent typhus.
Discuss the chronic carrier state of typhoid with patients and recommend cholecystectomy if treatment with flouroquinolones fails.
Chloramphenicol (at 150 mg/kg every day for 5 days) is the only antibiotic that can be used in pregnancy to treat typhus fever and typhoid fever due to the teratogenic effects of doxycycline.
Treatment for typhus and typhoid are age dependent.
For children under the age of 8, treat the patient using chloramphenicol 150 mg/kg every day for 5 days.
For children over the age of 8, treat the patient with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 to 15 days or chloramphenicol 500 mg four times daily for 7 to 15 days.
Azithromycin can be used for scrub typhus in children.
